data.name: UFO: Aftershock
data.detailed_description:
UFO: Aftershock is a combination of tactical squad combat and global strategy that enhances and expands upon its prequel, UFO: Aftermath.

It is the year 2054. Fifty years after the disaster. Fifty years after the surface of Earth became uninhabitable. Retreating to the flying haven of the Laputa the remnants of humankind clung onto existence. Then a revolt against the increasingly rigid and corrupt human leadership of the Laputa escalated into a conflict that destroyed the colony. Now, the remaining survivors flee once again. Can they reclaim the Earth from the unknown forces that chased them into the skies?

Key features:

  • Intertwining global strategy and small scale tactical missions
  • Strategic resource and base management
  • Enhanced SAS (Simultaneous Action System) and RPG system in tactical play
  • Fight your way through multi-level buildings, inside and out
  • New amazing items and technologies to research and develop
  • Radical new training and experience system
  • New terrifying enemies and powerful allies
  • Added diplomacy element
  • New gripping storyline
  • Interactive destructible environment

reviews.review:
This is a real-time X-COM clone. That statement says a lot with only a few words. The thing is, it would be accurate for the predecessor to this game, UFO: Aftermath. This one does have some changes, mainly streamlining:
- Your characters have three movement modes: running, crouching and crawling. There is no stamina to worry about.
- Two aiming modes are available, fast and slow. There is barely a difference between the two.
- There is single shot, burst, and full auto fire, if I am not mistaken.
- You still have a maximum of seven characters deployed at any given time.

This is really all. The result is that the missions tend to be very simplistic and repetitive: you move your soldiers forward, see enemies, the enemies start closing the distance while you shoot at them. Of course, you may close the distance, as well. In fact, you have to do it at least a little because your accuracy falls off dramatically when at what appear to be fairly short distances. Since action all occurs simultaneously, it seems optimal to just let everyone shoot as much as possible constantly.

This would all be fine, if it were not for the structure of the campaign. It has a real stop-and-go rhythm, because you can and will be in situations where you have 3+ missions available simultaneously, to be undertaken with no time at all passing on the campaign map, followed by a period of zero activity for about a day. Interceptors and the skyranger from X-COM are not a factor here, though you do have a mobile base which kind of acts as the latter. This means that you are generally sitting there, doing nothing, until you spring into action once a mission appears.

This is pretty much all there is to say. As much as I like real-time-tactics games, this one just seems so very small-scale and simplistic that there is really nothing to keep me coming back after a few hours. Research lasting only 12 hours sounds like it should not take long, but depending on how many missions you wish to do, it could take real-world hours. And the missions don't really give you anything, I am sure that you could just hold a region such as Western Europe, and ignore everything else, simply sitting there and researching things until the end of the game. The campaign of X-COM collapsed to simplicity if you knew what you were doing, but this game seems even less impressive. The only real positive is that shooting things is satisfying, as enemies ragdoll. Pulling off flanking manoeuvres and concentrating fire on tight hallways can definitely be fun, but I just always get the feeling that there are more complex and interesting games I could play to get that experience.
